title: Catherine of Siena (1347–1380)
hook: a dyer's daughter who cared for plague victims and wrote hard letters to popes

segments.voice: Yesterday, Clare of Assisi, who fought for the right to own nothing. Your line was poor and glad. What did you clear out, and did you feel lighter? Day eighty-nine.

Imagine being the twenty-fourth of twenty-five children. That's Catherine. Her father dyes wool in the Italian city of Siena, and the house smells of vats and wet cloth and is never, ever quiet. Her parents want her married. She wants to give her whole life to God. So, at about sixteen, she cuts off her hair, and her furious family makes her do the housework like a servant. She doesn't fight them. She just decides, she says later, to build a room inside herself where she can always be with God, whatever her hands are doing. Today: the dyer's daughter who ended up telling popes what to do.
screen: `TWENTY-FOURTH OF TWENTY-FIVE.` → `A DYER'S HOUSE IN SIENA.` → `A ROOM INSIDE HERSELF.`

segments.voice: Catherine joined a group of Dominican laywomen who wore the habit but lived at home. For three years she hardly left her little room, praying. Then, she said, she was sent out. When plague swept Siena, she nursed the sick others were afraid to touch. She walked with a young man condemned to death all the way to the executioner's block, and held his head. And then she started writing letters. She couldn't write well herself for most of her life, so she dictated them, sometimes several at once, to friends taking turns. Nearly four hundred survive, to tailors, soldiers, queens and popes. Here's the context. For about seventy years, the popes had lived not in Rome but in Avignon, in France. Catherine thought the pope belonged in Rome, with his flock. So she wrote to Pope Gregory the Eleventh, bluntly and lovingly. She called him, in Italian, something like sweet daddy, and then told him to be a man, stop being afraid, and come back. She even traveled to Avignon to say it to his face. In 1377, he went back to Rome. She died three years later, at thirty-three. In 1970 the Church named her one of the first two women Doctors of the Church. And today's line? People often quote her as saying: be who God meant you to be and you will set the world on fire. That's a modern paraphrase. What she actually wrote to a friend was closer to: if you are what you should be, you'll set all of Italy on fire. Either way, the point is hers.
screen: `NURSING THE SICK, HOLDING A HEAD.` · `NEARLY FOUR HUNDRED LETTERS.` · `COME BACK TO ROME.` · `A DOCTOR OF THE CHURCH.` · then, large: `IF YOU ARE WHAT YOU SHOULD BE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say one true thing kindly. Settle and breathe. Think of something you've been needing to say to someone: a hard truth, a boundary, a worry about them. Catherine was blunt, but she wrapped her bluntness in love. Picture saying it, simply, with warmth, no sarcasm, no speech. Choose the first sentence. Let it be kind and true at once. And remember her room inside: if you pray, you can go there now, and ask for courage. The bell holds the time.
Catherine of Siena. A dyer's daughter who nursed plague victims, dictated hundreds of letters, and told a pope to come home. Today's word.
Your line: be who god meant. Today, say the one true thing, kindly, to the person who needs to hear it. Day eighty-nine.

howItsDone: Catholics keep the feast of Saint Catherine of Siena on 29 April; she is a patron of Italy and of Europe, and her letters and her book, the Dialogue, are still read as guides to prayer.

what it means: a laywoman who nursed the sick, dictated nearly four hundred letters, and told a pope, lovingly, to come home.
what a scholar hears: the Avignon papacy, 1309 to 1377. her famous line is a paraphrase of a letter: if you are what you should be, you'll set all Italy on fire.

notes: All Catherine material is paraphrased; no quotations used.
Birth order: usually 'the 24th of 25 children' (her twin Giovanna died in infancy). Confirm.
Age at cutting her hair ('about sixteen') and the family's punishment are from Raymond of Capua; the 'inner cell' image is hers. Confirm.
The condemned young man was Niccolò di Toldo (1375); she received his head. Confirm.
Letters: about 380 survive. She is traditionally said to have learned to write late in life. Confirm.
'Sweet daddy' renders 'dolce babbo mio' in her letters to Gregory XI; 'be a man' reflects 'virile' language in the letters. Confirm the paraphrase is fair.

Carry 'be who god meant' comes from a popular paraphrase; the script explains the original (Letter 368 to Stefano Maconi: 'Se sarete quello che dovete essere, metterete fuoco in tutta Italia'). Confirm the letter number.
Doctor of the Church 4 October 1970, a week after Teresa of Ávila; co-patron of Italy (1939) and Europe (1999). Confirm.
